history.hook_sig: most caching advice you read assumes a single
texts: Most caching advice you read assumes a single server and low traffic. That world died years ago. At scale the rules invert: the hard part is not invalidation, it is coherence across tiers. Here are three lessons learned from a payment platform that processes 50k requests per second.

Lesson one: TTL based expiry causes thundering herds. When a hot key expires every client hits the database at once. We switched to probabilistic early refresh. Each client rolls a die on read, if the roll hits a threshold it refreshes in the background. The herd disappears, latency p99 drops forty percent.

Lesson two: Redis is not a silver bullet. Network round trips add up. We added a tiny in process LRU cache in front of Redis for the hottest thousand keys. Hit rate on the local tier is ninety two percent. Redis CPU dropped sixty percent. The extra complexity is two hundred lines of code and a config flag.

Lesson three: Cache coherence beats cache size. We version every cached object with a monotonic counter stored in Postgres. On write we increment the counter and publish the new version to a compacted Kafka topic. Readers poll the topic and evict stale entries locally. Zero stale reads, no distributed locks, no magic.

texts: I chose Cassandra for the write path because the team said "we need linearizable reads." Six months later the on-call rotation was burning out debugging tombstone compaction storms at 3am. The requirement was never linearizable reads. It was "patient records must never lose an update." Different constraint, totally different database.

The constraint-first framework has three axes. Consistency model: what happens when two writes race. Latency budget: p99 ceiling the product cannot exceed. Operational complexity: who runs this at 3am and how many people does it take. Pick one as non-negotiable. The other two bend around it.

If consistency is non-negotiable you get Postgres, Spanner, FoundationDB. You pay in write latency and operational depth. If latency is non-negotiable you get Redis, Scylla, Aerospike. You pay in consistency guarantees and data modeling rigidity. If operations is non-negotiable you get managed Postgres, DynamoDB, Cloud SQL. You pay in cost and vendor lock-in.

The trap is pretending you can maximize all three. A fintech ledger chose Spanner because "we need SQL and global consistency." Their p99 write latency hit 800ms. A gaming leaderboard chose Redis because "we need sub-millisecond." They lost score updates during failover. Both teams knew the tradeoff. Neither named it upfront.

texts: constrained decision: given a user-facing workflow with strict latency needs and occasional downstream failures, when would you add a queue-and what constraint would change your answer?

picture this: a user hits "place order" on your checkout page. you have 200ms p99 to respond. downstream you call a payment gateway that fails 2% of the time with 500s, and an inventory service that times out 1% of the time. both are idempotent. do you call them synchronously from the request thread, or push to a queue and respond "processing"?

sync path: user gets immediate success or failure. 200ms budget means you have ~150ms for both calls after network overhead. a single timeout blows your SLA. retries from the client mean duplicate charges unless you built idempotency keys everywhere. but when it works, it's fast and simple.

queue path: you accept the order, return 202 accepted, and a background worker processes payment then inventory. retries, exponential backoff, dead-letter queues-all handled without user involvement. cost: you added 50-100ms of queue latency minimum, plus the user must poll or websocket for final status. complexity moved from client to infra.

my rule: if p99 latency budget minus network overhead leaves <100ms for downstream calls, queue is off the table-sync with aggressive timeouts and client-side idempotency keys. if you have >150ms headroom and downstream failure rate >0.5%, queue wins. what's your cutoff?

texts: We shipped a checkout service with a hard p99 latency budget of 120ms. The database could do p99 80ms on a good day, but under load it spiked to 400ms. We put Redis in front with a 5-second TTL. Cache hit: 2ms. Cache miss: 400ms plus the Redis round trip.

The failure mode we didn't model: Redis network partition. When the cache became unavailable, every request fell through to the database simultaneously. The thundering herd took the primary from 80ms p99 to 2.3 seconds. We lost the latency budget and the error budget in the same minute.

We added a local in-memory fallback with a 500ms TTL and a circuit breaker that fails open to stale local data after 3 consecutive Redis timeouts. Now a Redis outage means 500ms of potentially stale reads instead of a full cascade. The tradeoff is explicit: 500ms staleness window, bounded by the local TTL.

The alternative was read-through with async refresh and a background job that keeps the cache warm. Simpler mental model, but the refresh job adds operational surface area and its own failure modes. We chose the local fallback because it fails deterministically and the staleness bound is visible in code, not in a cron schedule.

history.hook_sig: stop using uuids as primary keys. they destroy
texts: Stop using UUIDs as primary keys. They destroy write performance, bloat indexes by 4x, and you almost certainly don't need them. Your database is paying a tax for a scale you will never hit.

A UUID v4 is 16 random bytes. InnoDB clusters data by primary key. Every insert lands on a random page. The buffer pool churns. The write-ahead log amplifies. I watched a 2 TB table go from 800 writes/sec to 3,200 writes/sec just by switching to BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT. Same hardware. Same workload.

"BUT what about merge conflicts across shards?" Use a 64-bit composite: (shard_id << 48) | local_sequence. Monotonic inside each shard, globally unique, zero coordination. Fits in 8 bytes. Sequential on disk. No application rewrite required.

"BUT UUIDs prevent ID enumeration attacks!" Your API should not expose internal primary keys anyway. Return opaque tokens (UUIDv7 or nanoid) at the boundary. Keep the cluster key sequential. Security at the edge, performance at the core.

UUIDs make sense when you generate IDs offline, on mobile, or across truly independent services with no shared sequence. That is not your monolith. Benchmark your write path this week. If the primary key is random, you are lighting money on fire. Prove me wrong.

texts: Stop using UUIDs as primary keys in high-write tables. They fragment the buffer pool, bloat indexes 4x, and turn range scans into random I/O. Your p99 latency pays the price.

A UUIDv4 is 16 random bytes. InnoDB clusters data by PK. Every insert lands on a random page. The working set explodes. A 10M row table with BIGINT fits in 2GB buffer pool. Same data with UUID needs 8GB just to keep the hot pages resident.

I learned this on a payments table doing 5K writes/sec. Switched PK from UUID to BIGINT. Index size dropped from 12GB to 3GB. Buffer pool hit rate jumped from 84% to 98%. P99 write latency fell from 45ms to 3ms. No code changes. Just the key type.

UUIDs have a place: distributed inserts without coordination, or when you need opaque IDs in URLs. But for the core tables taking the write load? They are a self-inflicted wound. Prove me wrong with your numbers.

history.hook_sig: i used uuidv4 for every primary key on
texts: I used UUIDv4 for every primary key on a payments service because "distributed systems need it." Two years later the buffer pool was 80 percent index pages. The table had 120 million rows. The primary key index alone was 18 GB. A BIGINT version of the same workload sat at 4.2 GB.

The difference is not magic. UUIDv4 is random. Every insert goes to a random leaf page. The B-tree fragments, pages split, the buffer pool churns. BIGINT inserts append to the rightmost page. Sequential writes, dense pages, minimal splits. On that workload the write throughput gap was 3.8x at peak.

But the caveats are real. If you shard by tenant and each shard stays under 50 million rows the index fits in RAM either way. If your write rate is under 5k inserts/sec the bottleneck is usually network or application code not the index. If you need globally unique IDs without coordination UUIDv4 is still the right call.

UUIDv7 fixes the locality problem. The timestamp prefix makes inserts mostly sequential. In the same test the index size dropped to 5.1 GB and write throughput matched BIGINT within 5 percent. The tradeoff: you lose pure randomness and gain a rough creation-time signal. For most OLTP workloads that is a feature not a bug.

texts: POSTGRES ON A SINGLE NODE HANDLES 100K WRITES PER SECOND IF YOU TUNE IT RIGHT. MOST TEAMS REACH FOR CASSANDRA OR SCYLLA BECAUSE THEY NEVER BOTHERED TO BENCHMARK THEIR ACTUAL WORKLOAD.

I ran the test on a boring c6i.4xlarge with gp3 storage. 50 million rows, 1KB each, async commit off, synchronous_commit = remote_apply, batch inserts of 5000 rows. Sustained 112k inserts/sec with p99 latency under 8ms. No sharding, no clustering, just Postgres.

history.hook_sig: benchmark challenge: how far can one postgres instance
texts:
Benchmark challenge: how far can one Postgres instance go before you actually need to split the write path?

I ran a reproducible write benchmark on a single node. Hardware: 8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, NVMe, Ubuntu 22.04, Postgres 16. Schema: one table, UUID PK, 5 indexed columns, no foreign keys. Workload: 100 concurrent clients, each doing INSERT + UPDATE on the same row set, 1 KB payload, autocommit on.

Results: sustained 42,000 writes/sec at p99 12 ms latency. CPU saturated at 95 percent sys, not user. The bottleneck was WAL fsync contention on the single NVMe device. No checkpoint storms, no bloat, no lock contention. Just the log device hitting its IOPS ceiling.

What moved the needle: synchronous_commit=off pushed it to 78k writes/sec with same latency profile. But that trades durability. Unlogged tables hit 110k. Partitioning the hot table across 4 partitions on the same disk added 15 percent by spreading WAL inserts. Parallel workers did nothing for this workload.

The honest answer: most teams hit application-layer bottlenecks (ORM overhead, N+1, missing indexes) long before Postgres taps out. I have not seen a real product workload that genuinely needs write sharding below 50k sustained writes/sec on modern hardware. Prove me wrong with your numbers.

texts:
BENCHMARK REVEAL: SAME WORKLOAD, SAME MACHINE, DISCLOSE THE SETUP BEFORE COMPARING UUID AND BIGINT

Postgres 17 on Ubuntu 24.04, 8 vCPU AMD EPYC, 32 GB RAM, NVMe. Shared buffers 8 GB, work_mem 256 MB, max_wal_size 4 GB. Table: id PK, payload jsonb, created_at timestamptz. No indexes beyond PK. WAL on same volume.

Workload: pgbench custom script, 50 concurrent clients, 10 minute runs, 3 warmup minutes discarded. Mix: 70% single-row inserts (returning id), 20% PK point lookups, 10% range scans of 100 rows by created_at. Autovacuum default. Each variant run 5 times, median reported.

UUID v4 (gen_random_uuid): median insert throughput 42,300 rows/sec, p99 insert latency 8.2 ms, table size 3.8 GB after 25M rows, index size 3.1 GB. BIGINT (identity): median insert throughput 78,900 rows/sec, p99 insert latency 3.1 ms, table size 2.1 GB, index size 1.4 GB. Page splits 4x higher on UUID.

Read path: PK point lookup p99 0.4 ms both (cached). Range scan 100 rows p99 1.2 ms BIGINT vs 2.8 ms UUID (index bloat). Sequential scan 1M rows 340 ms BIGINT vs 590 ms UUID. The write tax compounds: more pages, more WAL, more vacuum cycles, larger backups.

Run the script on your hardware, post your numbers: workload shape, row width, concurrent writers, p99 target. I will aggregate into a community dataset. Follow @owlsky17 so you don't miss the next one.

texts: Your ORM's default connection pool size is silently killing your p99 latency. Most frameworks ship with 10-20 connections. Your database can handle hundreds. The mismatch queues requests before they even hit the engine.
A Java service at 5k RPS sat at p99 800ms. CPU was 15%. The pool was 20 connections. We raised it to 200. p99 dropped to 45ms. No code changes. No schema changes. One config knob.

The formula is not magic. Target connections = (core count * 2) + effective spindle count. For SSD on 16 cores: 32-64. For Aurora with 1000 max_connections: 200-400 per app instance. Monitor wait_event_type = ClientRead. That is your queue signal.

Pool sizing is the highest leverage config change most teams never touch. They add read replicas, caching layers, and rewrite queries. The pool was the bottleneck the whole time. What is your current pool size and max_connections setting?

history.hook_sig: a larger connection pool made my database slower,
texts: A larger connection pool made my database slower, not faster. The team swore by 100 connections per service. p99 latency was 380ms under load. We dropped to 15 and it fell to 95ms. The fix was not the number itself, it was measuring where the database stopped scaling.

Here is how to find your real saturation point. Spin up a single replica of your production database. Use wrk or k6 with a fixed query set that mirrors your hottest endpoints. Incrementally raise concurrent connections from 1 to N. Record p99 latency at each step. The curve is the truth.

At low concurrency, latency stays flat and throughput grows. Then it bends. That bend is where adding more connections costs more in scheduling and lock contention than it gains in parallelism. In my case the bend was at 12. Beyond 20, latency climbed fast. The pool was a queue amplifier, not a throughput booster.

Most teams never see this because they test with idle databases and synthetic loads that never touch contention. Measure under realistic pressure, with warmup, with cache cold, with the noisy neighbors your queries actually fight. Pool size is not a config to copy from a blog.

What is your pool-sizing method? Did you measure the bend, or did you inherit the default? Share your worst latency surprise and I will dig into it next.

texts: Most engineers reach for new indexes when a query is slow. The counterintuitive move: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE first and compare estimated rows versus actual rows. A 100x gap means the planner is hallucinating. Fix the statistics, not the schema.

I watched a payments query scan 2 million rows to return 12. The plan estimated 50 rows. The culprit was a stale pg_statistic entry on a correlated column. ANALYZE fixed it in 400ms. The index would have taken 4 hours to build and changed nothing.

Run this on your slow query:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT ...
Look at the rows= estimate versus actual rows= in each node. If actual exceeds estimate by more than 10x, the planner chose the wrong join order or scan type because it misunderstood the data distribution.

Common causes of estimation drift: correlated columns without extended statistics, skewed values without histograms, recent bulk loads without ANALYZE, and partition pruning failures. Each leaves a distinct fingerprint in the plan. Learn the fingerprints and you stop guessing.

history.hook_sig: production symptom that bites every team: you increase
texts: Production symptom that bites every team: you increase the connection pool to fix throughput, and p99 latency gets worse. The database is not the bottleneck. Your requests are queueing for connections that do not exist yet.

The pool grows, new connections handshake, TLS negotiates, the OS schedules the thread. Meanwhile the request sits in the client-side queue. That wait time is invisible to your APM because it happens before the span starts. You see healthy DB latency, angry users.

How to tell which queue owns the pain. Instrument two timers at the client: time from request start to connection acquired, and time from query sent to first row. If the first timer dominates p99, you are connection-starved. If the second dominates, the DB is slow.

Quick diagnostic you can run in prod today. Add a histogram for pool wait time. Alert when p99 pool wait exceeds 50 ms. Correlate with active connection count. If they rise together while DB CPU is flat, the pool size is the problem, not the database.

history.hook_sig: high p99 latency does not mean your queries
texts: High p99 latency does not mean your queries are slow. It means sessions are stuck waiting for something, and most teams waste weeks chasing the wrong bottleneck. Here is how to tell the difference in 3 minutes.

Check pg_stat_activity where state = 'active'. If you see a swarm of sessions all running the same query but p99 is sky-high, the queries are likely slow. But if active sessions are few and p99 is still bad, the bottleneck is upstream: connection-pool exhaustion or lock contention.

Run this query: select wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*) from pg_stat_activity where wait_event is not null group by wait_event_type, wait_event order by count desc. If you see a flood of 'Lock', 'LWLock', or 'BufferPin' waits, your queries are slow. If you see 'Client', 'Socket', or 'Timeout' waits dominating, your connection pool is exhausted.

The tell: connection-pool exhaustion shows up as sessions sitting idle in transaction or waiting on Client/Socket events. Slow queries show up as long-running active states with heavy CPU or I/O wait events. One is a resource-starvation problem, the other is a query-efficiency problem. Fix the wrong one and you will stay stuck.

Which wait event shows up most in your production pg_stat_activity dumps? Drop the exact wait_event_type and wait_event you are seeing. If you are unsure, run the query above and paste your top three rows.

history.hook_sig: if api p99 is rising while postgres cpu
texts: If API p99 is rising while Postgres CPU stays low, check pool wait time before adding database capacity. Most teams scale the wrong layer.

The symptom looks like a database problem. Latency climbs, errors spike, on-call gets paged. But `pg_stat_activity` shows idle connections, CPU is at 15 percent, and query plans look fine. The real bottleneck is invisible in standard dashboards.

Your application spends milliseconds waiting for a free connection from the pool. That wait time adds directly to p99 but never shows up in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`. The database executes fast. The queue to reach it does not.

Measure it: instrument your pool library to record `wait_time_ms` per request. In HikariCP enable `poolStatsLogInterval`. In Go `database/sql` wrap `Conn()` with timing. Plot p99 wait time alongside p99 query time. They diverge when the pool is undersized.
Fix it: raise `maximumPoolSize` until wait-time p99 drops below 1ms. Then tune `minimumIdle` to absorb bursts without new connection overhead. One config change, measurable result, no new hardware.

history.hook_sig: production symptom: requests are slow but database cpu
texts: Production symptom: requests are slow but database CPU sits at 15 percent. You check slow queries, nothing obvious. The engine is idle. The real bottleneck is the connection pool queueing work before it ever reaches Postgres.

The diagnostic split is two numbers. Pool wait time: how long a request waits for a connection. Query time: how long the statement actually runs. If pool wait dominates, adding indexes or tuning SQL will not move p99. You are optimizing the wrong layer.

Measure it in production. Wrap the pool borrow with a histogram: timestamp at checkout, timestamp at query start. The delta is queue time. In Postgres enable log_min_duration_statement = 0 briefly or use pg_stat_statements with a client-side wrapper. The gap tells the whole story.

When queue time exceeds query time you have three levers. Increase pool size until CPU saturates. Add a read replica for SELECT-heavy paths. Or push backpressure to the load balancer with a request queue and timeout. Re-measure the same two metrics to confirm the fix.

texts: Most engineers still treat EXPLAIN ANALYZE like a checkbox. They look at the plan shape, nod, and move on. The real signal isnt the plan shape. It is the gap between estimated rows and actual rows. That gap tells you exactly why the optimizer picked a bad path.

Postgres defaults statistics target to 100. On a column with 10 million distinct values that captures 0.001 percent of the distribution. The optimizer sees a flat line and assumes uniform distribution. Your query asks for a hot key. The plan expects 50 rows. Reality returns 500,000. Nested loops melt the CPU.

First check: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the slow query. Find the node with the widest estimated vs actual rows ratio. Ignore cost numbers. A ratio above 10x on any join or filter node means your statistics are lying to the planner. That is the smoking gun.

Fix: raise statistics target on the skewed column to 1000 or create extended statistics on the correlated columns. ANALYZE afterward. Re run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The ratio collapses. The planner switches to a hash join or bitmap scan. Latency drops 10x without a single index change.

texts: Most engineers run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and glance at the plan. They miss the number that actually matters: estimated rows versus actual rows. A ratio above 10x means the planner is guessing, and every index you add after that is a shot in the dark.

Last month a reporting query on our orders table hit 12 seconds. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a nested loop join with estimated rows 1, actual rows 47,000. Ratio 47,000x. The planner thought a customer filter would return one row. It returned forty-seven thousand because statistics were stale after a bulk insert.

The fix was not a new index. It was ANALYZE orders; then the same query ran in 40 milliseconds. The planner switched to a hash join because it finally knew the true cardinality. No schema change, no code deploy, two seconds of maintenance work.

Next time a query is slow, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and divide actual rows by estimated rows for the driving table. If the ratio exceeds 10, stop adding indexes. Run ANALYZE on the underlying tables first. The planner cannot optimize what it cannot measure.

texts: diagnostic misconception: accurate row estimates do not mean a query is fast. check BUFFERS to see whether it is reading from disk

most engineers stop at rows estimated versus rows actual. they see a 1.2x ratio and call it good. but the planner can nail the row count and still choose a plan that hammers the storage layer. the real latency signal lives in shared read versus shared hit

run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and look at the Buffers line. shared hit means cache. shared read means disk. a query with perfect estimates and 50,000 shared reads will stall under load while the same plan with 50,000 shared hits flies

concrete next step: if shared read is high, check whether the working set fits in shared_buffers. then verify effective_io_concurrency and random_page_cost match your storage. the fix is often config, not indexes

history.hook_sig: diagnostic blind spot: a large gap between estimated
texts: diagnostic blind spot: a large gap between estimated and actual rows is a clue, not a verdict. Most engineers see 1000x ratio and immediately reach for CREATE INDEX. The planner is not lying to you. It is working with stale data. The fix starts with pg_stat_clear_snapshot and a fresh ANALYZE, not a new index.

your EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Seq Scan with rows=1 actual=50000. Classic estimate miss. Before you touch indexes, run this:

SELECT schemaname, tablename, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze, n_dead_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'public';

If last_analyze is hours or days old while n_dead_tup keeps climbing, autovacuum is not keeping up. That is your real bottleneck.

autovacuum defaults are conservative. For high-churn tables, tune per-table:

ALTER TABLE orders SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01,
  autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.005,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 2,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000
);

Lower scale factors trigger analyze sooner. Lower cost_delay with higher cost_limit lets it work faster without starving queries. Monitor pg_stat_progress_vacuum to verify it runs.

after ANALYZE, re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Same plan? Estimate now close to actual? Good. The planner can now cost alternatives correctly. If it still picks a bad plan, then and only then consider indexes, statistics targets, or extended statistics. The order matters: fresh stats first, schema changes second.
